title: the Mandukya Karika (Gaudapada)
hook: a coil on a dim path makes a walker's heart jump. a flashlight shows a rope. Gaudapada asks where the snake went

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mandukya Karika opened: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth, with Om laid over all of it.
screen: `THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: THREE ROOMS AND A FOURTH.` · `A WEEK TO LOOK BACK ON.`

segments.voice: A man is coming home late, down a dim side path. Something lies coiled across the stones. A snake. His body reacts before he can think: a jump, a cold flush, a step back. He finds his phone and turns on the light. It's a rope. He laughs, a little too loud. And then, if he's the kind of person who wonders, a strange question arrives. Where did the snake go? It made his heart pound; it was real enough for that. Gaudapada asks this question in the Mandukya Karika, and his answer reaches back across the whole week.
screen: `A COIL ON THE PATH.` → `THE LIGHT: A ROPE.` → `WHERE DID THE SNAKE GO?`

segments.voice: First, the week. Six days with Shankara on the Brahma Sutra's first four lines, and his word jnana, the knowing that undoes a mix-up. Then Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya, with its three states and the fourth. Today the two threads meet, because tradition places Gaudapada before Shankara, in Shankara's own lineage, and the mix-up gets a vivid picture in his verses. One section of the Karika asks how real the world people see is. He starts with dreams. Inside a dream there are cities, roads, whole days of travel, and yet it all happens inside the sleeper. On waking, it's gone. Then the bold move: what isn't there at the beginning and isn't there at the end, he says, isn't truly there in the middle either. Now the rope. A rope, not seen clearly in the dark, is imagined as a snake, or as a stream of water, or as other things. When the rope is seen for what it is, the imagining stops. In the same way, he says, the self is imagined as all kinds of things, and when the self is known, the imagining ends. Notice what he doesn't say. The snake didn't turn into the rope, or crawl away. It was never anything apart from the rope. Gaudapada's reading is a hard one, and some other schools of Vedanta answer it: they hold the world to be real, the work of the Lord.
screen: `A WEEK OF JNANA, THEN THE MANDUKYA.` · `NOT AT THE START, NOT AT THE END.` · `THE ROPE TAKEN FOR A SNAKE.` · `THE SNAKE WAS NEVER APART FROM IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small worry that has been coiled on your path this week. Don't push it away; look at it the way you'd shine a light on something in the dark, and ask gently: what is actually here? Then let the question rest and come back to the breath; if you pray, hold the worry up to the light you pray to.
The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, where a rope seen in the dark as a snake stands for the self taken for all kinds of things.
Your line: the Mandukya Karika, Gaudapada. The snake never went anywhere; it was never apart from the rope. That's day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Advaita Vedanta teachers use the rope and the snake to explain how the world can be taken for something it isn't, and students reflect on the image in study and meditation.

chat.who: a friend walking home with you
chat.says: In Gaudapada's rope-and-snake picture, where does the snake go when the light comes on?
options: Nowhere: it was never anything apart from the rope; only the imagining stops.
It crawls away into the dark, and might come back another night.
It was a real snake, and the rope was what he imagined instead.
chat.meaning: For Gaudapada, the rope taken for a snake shows the self imagined as many things; when the self is known, the imagining ends.

Gaudapada.meaning: the teacher tradition credits with the Mandukya Karika

Mandukya.meaning: a short Upanishad on Om and the states of the self

Shankara.meaning: the great teacher of Advaita Vedanta

Vedanta.meaning: the schools that read the Upanishads and the Brahma Sutras

jnana.meaning: knowing, and the way of freedom through knowing

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 2.1–2.6 (dream objects seen within the body; what is absent at the beginning and the end is so in the middle too)
Mandukya Karika 2.17–2.18 (a rope not clearly seen is imagined as a snake, a line of water and so on; when the rope is ascertained the imagining ceases; so with the self)
